issues.legal_issue: In an eviction suit founded on a landlord–tenant relationship, the court determines whether that relationship exists and may consider title only incidentally rather than finally.
material_facts: The claimant brought an eviction suit after purchasing the premises from a person said to have inherited them from the former owner.
The tenant had attorned to the claimant, agreed to pay rent, and paid rent for two months.
An adoption deed and the tenant’s failure to dispute the adoption supported a prima facie basis for the transferor’s succession to the private property.
issues.conclusion: The claimant was established as the landlord and the respondent as the tenant; the title inquiry was only prima facie and collateral, not a final adjudication of title.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 3(III) and (VII) of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent & Eviction) Act, 1950, a landlord includes a person entitled to receive rent and a tenant includes a person liable to pay it. In an eviction suit based on the relationship of landlord and tenant, title is not the primary issue; the court makes only a prima facie decision on the collateral question of landlord status. The court relied on L.I.C. v. India Automobiles & Co. and distinguished Rajendra Singh v. Union of India, which held that recognition as ruler did not itself recognize private-property rights. The adoption deed and the surrounding facts supported prima facie succession to the private property.

predicates.eviction_suit: The claimant brought a proceeding seeking eviction of a person occupying premises as a tenant.
predicates.tenant_attorned_to_claimant: The occupant accepted the claimant as landlord and agreed to pay rent to the claimant.
predicates.claimant_has_prima_facie_basis_for_rent_: The claimant presented evidence supporting an entitlement to receive rent from the occupant.

issues.definition: When an eviction suit is based on tenancy and the occupant has accepted the claimant as landlord, evidence supporting the claimant’s entitlement to rent establishes the landlord–tenant relationship without finally determining title.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court hearing a second appeal cannot reappreciate evidence and replace supported factual findings of the lower courts without a substantial question of law.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court found that the claimant had a genuine and bona fide need for the premises.
The High Court reversed that finding after reappreciating the evidence but formulated no substantial question of law.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in reappreciating the evidence or substituting its findings on bona fide need.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100(1) and (4) of the Code of Civil Procedure permit a second appeal only where the case involves a substantial question of law, which the High Court must formulate. An erroneous appreciation of evidence or a disagreement with a factual finding does not by itself permit interference. The court relied on Ramachandra v. Ramalingam and Bhagwan Das v. Jiley Kaur.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding before the High Court is a second appeal from a decree made in appeal by a subordinate court.
predicates.lower_courts_made_supported_factual_find: The lower courts made factual findings after assessing the evidence, including a finding on the claimant’s need for the premises.
predicates.no_substantial_question_of_law_formulate: The High Court did not formulate a substantial question of law as the basis for disturbing the factual findings.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, supported factual findings of the lower courts remain undisturbed when the High Court has formulated no substantial question of law.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s denial of the landlord’s title may furnish a ground for eviction when the landlord has a prima facie basis for entitlement and the denial is not bona fide.
material_facts: The tenant denied the claimant’s title after the claimant acquired the premises from a person who had a prima facie basis for succession to the property.
The tenant had not disputed the asserted adoption in replying to the notice, but denied the claimant’s title and the tenancy relationship.
issues.conclusion: The tenant’s denial of the claimant’s title was not bona fide and furnished a ground for eviction.
issues.legal_principle: In an eviction suit, the court may examine the tenant’s contention about title to determine whether the denial is bona fide, but does not finally decide title. The court applies the principles in L.I.C. v. India Automobiles & Co. and the governing rent-control law concerning the landlord–tenant relationship.

rule.if: eviction_suit and tenant_denied_landlord_title and landlord_has_prima_facie_entitlement and denial_lacks_bona_fide_basis

predicates.eviction_suit: The landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction of a tenant from premises.
predicates.tenant_denied_landlord_title: The tenant disputed the landlord’s title to the premises.
predicates.landlord_has_prima_facie_entitlement: The landlord presented evidence supporting an entitlement to receive rent from the tenant.
predicates.denial_lacks_bona_fide_basis: The tenant’s denial was unsupported by a bona fide basis in the circumstances of the case.

issues.definition: In an eviction suit, a tenant’s denial of title furnishes a ground for eviction when the landlord has prima facie entitlement and the denial lacks a bona fide basis.

issues.legal_issue: A concurrent finding that the landlord would suffer greater comparative hardship is not open to interference in a second appeal, particularly where the tenant provides no evidence that alternative accommodation is unavailable.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court found, after comparing the parties’ circumstances, that the landlord would suffer greater hardship if eviction were refused.
The tenant presented no evidence that alternative accommodation could not be obtained in the town.
The High Court disturbed the concurrent hardship finding in the second appeal.
issues.conclusion: The concurrent finding that the landlord would suffer greater hardship should have been accepted and was not open to challenge in the second appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Comparative hardship is a factual question; a concurrent finding on it is not open to interference in a second appeal absent a proper basis for such interference. A tenant claiming greater hardship must show that alternative accommodation cannot be obtained in the relevant town. The court relied on Bega Begum v. Abdul Ahad Khan and the limits on second appeals under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding before the High Court is a second appeal from a decree made in appeal by a subordinate court.
predicates.lower_courts_found_landlord_would_suffer: The lower courts compared the parties’ circumstances and found that refusing eviction would cause greater hardship to the landlord.
predicates.tenant_provided_no_evidence_alternative_: The tenant did not present evidence that alternative accommodation could not be obtained in the relevant town.

issues.definition: A concurrent finding that the landlord would suffer greater hardship stands in a second appeal when the tenant has not shown that alternative accommodation is unavailable.
